To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the Brady-Spense prediction of a 1981 earthquake in Peru was widely reported in the scientific and popular press, and that the reaction of the scientific community was overwhelmingly negative.

(a) the Brady-Spense prediction of a major earthquake in Peru for 1981 was a paradigm-changing prediction, and that (b) the response to it by the scientific community was a textbook example of the kind of response that Kuhn (1977) says paradigm-changing research frequently engenders.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the scientific community was not prepared to accept the Brady-Spense prediction as valid, and that the scientific community did not react well when it was not accepted.
the Brady-Spense prediction, and the reaction of the earthquake science community to this prediction, is an excellent illustration of the Kuhnian process of paradigm shift.

the Brady-Spense prediction and its aftermath are illustrative of the difficulties in predicting earthquakes and of the problems in communicating the results of earthquake prediction research to the public and the scientific community.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the Brady-Spense prediction, and the response it elicited from the seismological community, can be viewed as a paradigm case of the social processes that have been observed to be associated with paradigm change in science.
the Brady-Spense prediction was a paradigm challenge that failed.
the scientific community is not monolithic, but is rather comprised of individuals with a wide range of views and values.
